brief.situation: 17:30 in a secured memory care unit. You are the nurse aide. Mrs. Halloran, 86, who has Alzheimer disease, has her coat on and is pulling at the locked exit door: 'I have to get the children from school, they'll be waiting.' Dinner is at 18:00 and the dining room is noisy.
handover: She walks without an aid and is usually calm in the morning. Late afternoons she is often restless.
Her care plan: approach from the front, use her name, she likes folding laundry and talking about her four children (now grown). Toileting every 2-3 hours; last toileted at 13:30.
The nurse is passing medications at the other end of the hall and answers if you call.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
What you say and do changes how upset she is; her mood is shown in words.
Partway through you are asked to write what you think is behind it. The case ends at 18:00, then a debrief scores what you did.

source.note: Left alone at the door, her distress climbs to a fall-risk struggle in about 40 min. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated behavioral model.
While she is engaged in something she likes, distress eases. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated behavioral model.
At this level she pushes past or pulls free and falls. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated behavioral model.
Calm enough to walk to dinner. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated behavioral model.
Authored target: unmet needs checked within 15 min. FLAG.
Authored target: the nurse told within 20 min. FLAG.

approach.label: Approach from the front, at her eye level; use her name and a calm, slow voice

effects.log: She turns to you: 'Oh, it's you. I'm late for the children.' (She is {mood}.)

reorient.label: Tell her the facts: her children are grown, it is 2026, and she lives here now

effects.log: 'That's a lie! Let me out!' She bangs the door. (She is {mood}.)

validate.label: Acknowledge the feeling: 'You're worried about them. Tell me about your children.'

effects.log: Her grip on the handle loosens. 'Four of them. Mary is the eldest, she minds the others.' (She is {mood}.)

redirect.label: Invite her to help you: 'Mary would want them to have clean towels. Will you help me fold?'
redirect.why: She is already busy with you.

then.log: She takes your arm and walks with you to the laundry basket in the quiet lounge.
'I don't have time for towels!' She turns back to the door. Her worry hasn't been heard yet.

needs.label: Check for unmet needs: bathroom, pain, hunger, thirst

effects.log: Her brief is soaked; you help her to the bathroom and change her. She winces and rubs her right hip when she sits: 'It aches.' You offer water; she drinks a full cup.

environment.label: Lower the stimulation: steer her away from the noisy dining room, lights up, shades drawn

effects.log: The lounge is quieter and brighter.

hold.label: Stand in front of the door and hold her wrists so she stops pulling

effects.log: She twists against your grip, crying out. Holding a resident to stop her moving is a physical restraint.

chair.label: Sit her in a recliner with the tray table locked across her until dinner

effects.log: She pushes at the tray and tries to climb out over the side. A tray she cannot remove is a physical restraint.

askSedative.label: Ask the nurse for something to calm her down before dinner

effects.log: Nurse: 'A drug to keep her quiet for us would be a chemical restraint. Tell me what you're seeing and what you've tried.'

report.label: Tell the nurse what you observed

then.log: You report what you saw: at the door at 17:30 asking for her children, soaked brief, a full cup of water, wincing and rubbing her right hip, and what calmed her. Nurse: 'Thank you. I'll assess the hip now.'
You tell the nurse she is 'acting up again'. Nurse: 'What exactly is she doing, and have you checked her needs?'

effects.log: She is shouting and yanking the handle; another resident starts crying.

why.question: What might be behind Mrs. Halloran's behavior, and how will you respond without making it worse?

parts.label: What is behind it
parts.criteria: Names late-day sundowning in dementia and looks for unmet needs (toileting, pain, thirst, noise) as causes; separates what was observed from what it might mean.
parts.modelAnswer: Late-afternoon restlessness in dementia, and possibly an unmet need: she hasn't been toileted since 13:30 and the dining room is noisy. I'll check the bathroom, pain and a drink, and report what I see, not a label.

parts.label: How to respond
parts.criteria: Calm approach from the front, validates the feeling instead of correcting her, redirects to something she likes, lowers stimulation; no holding, no locked tray, no drug for convenience; tells the nurse the observations.
parts.modelAnswer: Approach calmly, use her name, don't argue that her children are grown. Acknowledge the worry, then invite her to fold towels in the quiet lounge. Never hold her or lock her in a chair, and never ask for a drug to keep her quiet. Tell the nurse exactly what I saw.

noProgress.rationale: Still distressed at the door after dinner has started is distress left unrelieved.

expertPath.text: Approach from the front, at eye level, with her name. Acknowledge the worry about her children; let her talk about them.
Invite her to fold towels in the quiet lounge, away from the dining room noise.
Bathroom: soaked brief; she winces at her right hip. A cup of water. Count her pulse.
Tell the nurse what you saw: the time, what she said, the wet brief, the hip, what calmed her.

fell.headline: She fell
fell.body: Correcting her reality or holding her back raised her distress until she pulled free. Calm, validate, redirect, and look for the need behind the behavior.

settled.headline: Settled without restraint
settled.body: You approached calmly, acknowledged her worry instead of correcting it, redirected her to something she likes, found the wet brief and the hip pain, and told the nurse what you saw. That is the expert path.

settledLate.headline: No fall, by a harder route
settledLate.body: Check whether you argued with her reality, held her or locked her in a chair, asked for a drug to quiet her, or left her needs unchecked.

time_up.headline: Still at the door
time_up.body: Behavior in dementia is often a need: look for it, validate, redirect.

scoring.modelReasoning: Late-afternoon restlessness in Alzheimer disease is sundowning, and behavior often signals an unmet need: she had not been toileted since 13:30, she was thirsty, and her hip hurt. Approach from the front with her name in a calm voice, and acknowledge the feeling rather than correcting the facts; arguing that her children are grown escalates her. Redirect to something she likes, folding towels, somewhere quieter. Holding her wrists or locking a tray across her chair are physical restraints, and a drug to keep her quiet would be a chemical restraint; federal rules forbid restraints for discipline or staff convenience. Report observations, not labels, so the nurse can assess the hip.
